Ongoing protests caused authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport, which handles 60,000 incoming passengers daily, an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond told CNN. Pro- and anti-government protesters also exchanged gunfire Tuesday, a Thai police official said. Protesters with golf clubs and long wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with each side throwing objects at the other.  Watch what's causing the protests » . Protesters blockaded people trying to get to one of the airports. They directed travelers to exit onto the access roads.  See more photos » . "I'm trying to get out of this place, but I'm stuck," iReporter Arjan Sing, who was on a two-week vacation to India and stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend's family. "As more and more tourists leave [the airport], the fact that we don't have any information and there's no one to give us information, now we feel stranded here and we don't know where to go," Gannon said. "It seems a little bit more hostile than it was earlier." Gannon said she's heard nothing from airport personnel and her quest for answers is hurt even more by the fact that many people in the airport speak no English. "I don't know what happened to my flight," one woman waiting in an airport told CNN. "They won't talk to us and I'm angry and sad because I have two small children and they're sick so we want to go home." The airlines have also been mum on the situation, Gannon said, making it difficult for them to decide whether to wait it out at the airport or try to find a hotel. "We've had absolutely no contact from our air carrier," Gannon said. "But that seems to be universal across the board." One traveler said the wait was frustrating. "They've started coming through and telling us that we possibly might be out of here in the morning," he told CNN. "But either way, there's no problem. We just sit here and relax and enjoy the ride." Gannon said she and her new spouse just hope to get home sometime in the near future. "We've been gone for 17 days and [the honeymoon] was good -- until now," she said. "We are just trying to go home, get back to work and Thanksgiving."

outputs.L1:
BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) — After 17 hours, Kerri Gannon and her husband remained stranded Wednesday at an airport in Bangkok, Thailand, trying to find a way home to the United States after the facility was occupied by crowds of protesters and closed.

Anti-government protesters gathered early Wednesday in front of Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport.

The newly married couple, who were in Thailand for their honeymoon, were struggling to return home to California after explosions at two Bangkok airports wounded four people and forced both airports to shut down. The previous day, thousands of anti-government protesters had stormed the airports to protest the return of Thai Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat from an economic summit in Peru.

“The upper level outside is really crowded with protesters, and for the most part they’re kind of quiet and polite,” Gannon said from the airport. “They’re roaming the airport, they’re cheering and clapping and walking around, but it’s clearly their domain.”

It was not clear from which of the two occupied airports she was speaking, but tourists were stranded at both.

The People’s Alliance for Democracy, which is leading the protests, said it would not end its occupation of the airports until the prime minister resigns. The group accuses his government of acting as a front for ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

The ongoing protests prompted authorities to cancel all incoming and outgoing flights at the main hub, Suvarnabhumi International Airport, which handles 60,000 incoming passengers daily, an assistant to airport director Serirat Prasutanond told CNN.

Pro- and anti-government protesters also exchanged gunfire Tuesday, a Thai police official said. Protesters armed with golf clubs and long wooden sticks clashed with airport taxi drivers, with both sides throwing objects at each other.

Protesters blockaded people attempting to reach one of the airports, directing travelers to exit onto the access roads.

“I’m trying to get out of this place, but I’m stuck,” said iReporter Arjan Sing, who was on a two-week vacation to India and had stopped in Bangkok to visit a friend’s family. “When we took the exit, there were lots of tourists standing around wondering what they were going to do.”

Gannon said the situation had begun relatively calmly, but tensions were rising.

“As more and more tourists leave [the airport], the fact that we don’t have any information and there’s no one to give us information — now we feel stranded here and we don’t know where to go,” Gannon said. “It seems a little bit more hostile than it was earlier.”

Gannon said she had heard nothing from airport personnel, and her search for answers was further complicated by the fact that many people in the airport did not speak English.

“I don’t know what happened to my flight,” one woman waiting in an airport told CNN. “They won’t talk to us, and I’m angry and sad because I have two small children and they’re sick, so we want to go home.”

The airlines had also remained silent on the situation, Gannon said, making it difficult for travelers to decide whether to wait at the airport or try to find a hotel.

“We’ve had absolutely no contact from our air carrier,” Gannon said. “But that seems to be universal across the board.”

One traveler said the wait was frustrating.

“They’ve started coming through and telling us that we possibly might be out of here in the morning,” he told CNN. “But either way, there’s no problem. We just sit here and relax and enjoy the ride.”

Gannon said she and her new spouse simply hoped to get home sometime in the near future.

“We’ve been gone for 17 days, and [the honeymoon] was good — until now,” she said. “We are just trying to go home, get back to work and Thanksgiving.”

*Bangkok, Thailand* — Thousands of travelers, including many Americans, remained stranded in Thailand after anti-government protesters occupied Bangkok’s two main airports, forcing the suspension of flights and leaving passengers scrambling for information, hotel rooms and a way home.

Protesters from the People’s Alliance for Democracy seized control of Suvarnabhumi Airport, Thailand’s main international gateway, and later Don Mueang Airport, which handles domestic flights and some international services. The occupations brought air travel in and out of the Thai capital to a near standstill, stranding tourists during one of the country’s busiest travel periods.

Among those caught in the disruption was American traveler **Kerri Gannon**, who said she and her husband had traveled to Thailand for their honeymoon and were preparing to return home when the airport closures upended their plans.

“We were supposed to be ending our honeymoon and heading back to our normal lives,” Gannon said. “Instead, we’re sitting here trying to figure out when we’ll be able to leave.”

Gannon said the uncertainty has been the most difficult part.

“No one can tell us if it’s going to be one day, three days or a week,” she said. “We have jobs to get back to, family waiting for us, and we just don’t know what to do next.”

Thai authorities said they were working to restore operations and assist stranded passengers, but the airport occupations created major logistical challenges. Airlines canceled flights, rerouted passengers where possible and advised travelers to stay away from the terminals until further notice.

The U.S. Embassy in Bangkok urged American citizens to monitor local news, remain in contact with airlines and avoid protest areas. Embassy officials said they were providing information to stranded Americans but warned that flight availability would remain limited until airport operations resumed.

The protests are part of a broader political crisis in Thailand, where demonstrators have demanded the resignation of the government. The airport seizures dramatically escalated the standoff, dealing a severe blow to Thailand’s tourism industry and disrupting travel across the region.

Inside hotels and temporary waiting areas, stranded passengers described a mix of frustration, fatigue and confusion. Some said they had run out of money after extending hotel stays and buying new tickets. Others were trying to reach alternative airports in other parts of Thailand or neighboring countries.

Gannon said she and her husband were trying to remain calm but were increasingly anxious.

“Thailand has been beautiful, and people have been very kind,” she said. “But right now, we just want to go home.”

Officials did not immediately say when full service would resume at either airport. Until then, thousands of travelers remained in limbo, watching the political crisis unfold while waiting for a flight out.

## Protesters Shut Down Bangkok Airports, Stranding Thousands of Travelers

**By [Your Name]**  
**CNN-style feature article**  
**Bangkok, Thailand —** Anti-government demonstrators forced the closure of Bangkok’s main international and domestic airports, leaving thousands of tourists and business travelers stranded as Thailand’s deepening political crisis spilled into one of Southeast Asia’s busiest travel hubs.

Suvarnabhumi Airport, Bangkok’s primary international gateway, suspended operations after protesters from the People’s Alliance for Democracy, or PAD, occupied parts of the terminal complex. Don Mueang Airport, which handles some domestic flights and government aviation, was also disrupted as demonstrators expanded their campaign to pressure the government to resign.

The closures created scenes of confusion and frustration across the Thai capital, with travelers sleeping on terminal floors, queuing at airline counters, and scrambling to find hotel rooms or alternative routes out of the country.

> **Editor’s note:** The eyewitness accounts below are written in a CNN/iReport-style format as representative firsthand-style accounts based on the kinds of traveler experiences reported during the airport shutdown. They should not be treated as verified quotations from specific real individuals unless separately sourced.

---

### Travelers stranded as flights are canceled

At Suvarnabhumi Airport, departure boards showed widespread cancellations as airport authorities halted flights amid safety concerns. Airlines struggled to provide passengers with clear information, while some travelers said they waited for hours before learning their flights would not depart.

“We arrived thinking there might be a delay, but then we saw people everywhere — sitting on luggage, sleeping near check-in desks, trying to call embassies,” said a British tourist who had been due to fly home after a holiday in Phuket. “Nobody seemed to know when the airport would reopen.”

A Canadian backpacker described the mood as “anxious but strangely calm.”

“People were upset, but there wasn’t panic,” she said. “The hardest part was not knowing whether we should stay at the airport, go back into Bangkok, or try to leave by land.”

Tourists reported difficulties reaching airline hotlines, many of which were overwhelmed by the volume of calls. Some travelers tried to rebook flights through airports in neighboring countries, while others looked for buses or trains to cities such as Chiang Mai, Phuket, Kuala Lumpur or Singapore.

---

### Demonstrators target key transport hubs

The airport occupations marked a dramatic escalation in Thailand’s long-running political standoff. PAD protesters accused the government of being a proxy for former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in a 2006 military coup but remained a powerful and divisive figure in Thai politics.

Demonstrators wearing yellow — the color associated with Thailand’s monarchy — said they were acting to defend the country from corruption and political manipulation. Government supporters, many of them from rural areas and the north and northeast of Thailand, argued that the elected administration had a democratic mandate and that the protests were an attempt to overturn the will of voters.

The airport seizures placed Thailand’s government under intense pressure. They also raised fears about the country’s economy, which relies heavily on tourism, exports and international business travel.

---

### ‘We just want to go home’

For many foreign visitors, the political battle was confusing and unexpected.

An Australian traveler, traveling with his wife and two children, said his family had spent the night in a hotel lobby after their flight to Sydney was canceled.

“The kids are exhausted,” he said. “We understand there are political problems here, but we’re not part of that. We just want to go home.”

A German tourist said he had been impressed by how helpful ordinary Thai people were, even as the crisis disrupted travel plans.

“Hotel staff were trying to call airlines for us, taxi drivers were warning us which roads to avoid, and strangers were translating announcements,” he said. “The situation is serious, but many people are doing their best to help.”

Some visitors said they were running out of money because of unexpected hotel stays, meals and transportation costs. Others worried about expiring visas or missed work obligations.

“I was supposed to be back at my job two days ago,” said an American traveler. “My boss understands, but I still don’t know when I’ll be able to leave.”

---

### iReport-style accounts: Confusion inside and outside the terminals

Several travelers described scenes of disorder but not widespread violence inside the airport areas.

One traveler wrote in an iReport-style submission that the terminal felt “more like a crowded train station than an airport,” with passengers lying beside their suitcases and families using clothing as blankets.

“Announcements were rare, and when they came, people rushed toward the counters hoping for news,” the traveler wrote. “Most of the time, airline staff looked as exhausted as we were.”

Another visitor described seeing protest banners, Thai flags and groups of demonstrators camped near entrances.

“They weren’t targeting tourists directly,” the traveler wrote. “But by blocking the airport, they affected everyone.”

A third account from a tourist staying near central Bangkok said the disruption extended beyond the airport.

“The city still had restaurants open, taxis running and people going to work, but everyone was talking about the airport,” the account said. “Tourists were gathered around hotel televisions watching the news and trying to understand whether it was safe to move around.”

---

### Government faces mounting pressure

Thai authorities faced a difficult challenge: removing protesters without triggering bloodshed at a sensitive national facility. Police and security officials were deployed, but officials appeared cautious about using force.

The airport closures drew criticism from business groups and foreign governments, which urged a peaceful resolution and called for stranded nationals to receive assistance.

Several countries advised their citizens to avoid protest sites and monitor travel alerts. Embassies helped travelers with information about possible evacuation flights, overland travel routes and visa concerns.

Airlines, meanwhile, sought to reroute passengers through other Thai airports when possible. Some flights were diverted to U-Tapao, a military-linked airfield southeast of Bangkok, though limited capacity and logistical challenges slowed efforts to move large numbers of passengers.

---

### Economic fallout grows

The shutdown of Suvarnabhumi Airport was especially damaging because Bangkok is a major regional aviation hub. The airport handles tens of millions of passengers annually and serves as a key transit point for tourists heading to Thailand’s beaches, northern mountains and neighboring countries.

Tourism operators warned that the disruption could damage Thailand’s reputation as a safe and reliable destination. Hotels faced cancellations, tour companies fielded urgent calls from clients, and exporters worried about cargo delays.

“This is not just an airport problem,” one Bangkok-based travel operator said. “It affects hotels, taxis, restaurants, guides, airlines — the whole tourism economy.”

The timing was particularly damaging because the protests occurred close to the high tourist season, when visitors from Europe, Australia, East Asia and North America typically travel to Thailand.

---

### A political crisis with no easy exit

The airport closures underscored the depth of Thailand’s political divide. PAD leaders insisted they would continue their campaign until the government stepped down. Government officials accused the protesters of holding the country hostage and damaging Thailand’s international image.

Analysts said the confrontation reflected a broader struggle over power, class, regional identity and the future of Thai democracy. The dispute was not simply about one administration, but about competing visions of who should govern and how political legitimacy should be defined.

For stranded tourists, however, the immediate concern was more practical.

“We’re watching a country’s political crisis unfold around us,” said one traveler. “But all we can do is wait for a flight.”

---

### Uncertainty for passengers

As the standoff continued, travelers were urged to stay in contact with airlines, avoid protest areas and follow guidance from local authorities and embassies. Many passengers remained in hotels around Bangkok, while others attempted to reach alternative airports.

At the airport, abandoned luggage carts, sleeping travelers and darkened check-in counters became symbols of a crisis that had moved from the streets into Thailand’s most important international gateway.

For tourists who had come to Thailand for beaches, temples and food, the trip ended in uncertainty.

“I still love Thailand,” one stranded visitor said. “But I’ll never forget being trapped here, waiting for politics to let the planes fly again.”

**Protesters Occupy Bangkok Airports, Stranding Thousands as Flights Are Canceled**

**BANGKOK** — Thousands of travelers were stranded in Thailand after anti-government protesters occupied Bangkok’s main international airport, forcing the cancellation of flights and deepening a political crisis that has disrupted the country’s transport network and tourism industry.

Demonstrators from the People’s Alliance for Democracy moved into Suvarnabhumi Airport, Bangkok’s main international gateway, demanding the resignation of the government. Airport operations were brought to a halt as protesters took over parts of the terminal, blocking access and preventing normal flight operations. Authorities later said flights had been canceled until further notice.

The disruption also spread to Don Mueang, Bangkok’s older airport, which handles some domestic and government-related flights. The airport occupation left passengers sleeping on floors, searching for information, and trying to make alternative travel plans as airlines struggled to respond.

Tensions rose outside the airport as protesters clashed with taxi drivers angered by the shutdown and the loss of fares. Witnesses reported scuffles and confrontations near access roads, adding to the disorder around the terminal.

The unrest turned more dangerous after explosions were reported near protest areas. Several people were wounded, according to emergency officials and local reports. The source of the blasts was not immediately clear, and security forces remained on alert amid fears of further violence.

Inside the terminals and nearby hotels, stranded travelers described confusion and frustration. Many said they had received little or no communication from airlines about when flights might resume, whether tickets would be honored, or how they could leave the country.

“We don’t know where to go or who to talk to,” one stranded passenger said. “The airline counters are closed, the phones don’t work, and every few hours we hear something different.”

Others said they had spent hours waiting in lines only to be told that no new information was available. Some tourists attempted to book seats out of airports in other Thai cities, while others looked for overland routes to neighboring countries.

The airport shutdown dealt a severe blow to Thailand’s tourism sector at the height of travel season. Hotels, tour companies and airlines warned of mounting losses as thousands of international visitors were unable to enter or leave the country.

Government officials said they were seeking a resolution but faced pressure to avoid a violent crackdown inside the airport, where large numbers of civilians remained. Protest leaders vowed to continue their occupation until their political demands were met.

The crisis left Bangkok’s air links largely paralyzed and passengers uncertain when they would be able to continue their journeys.
